newsitem.title: GERMANY: Analysts' views on 1996 German bank results. [CORRECTED 11:57 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Analysts' views on 1996 German bank results. [CORRECTED 11:57 GMT]

text.p: The following are analysts' comments on preliminary 1996 earnings reports by Deutsche Bank AG and Bayerische Vereinsbank AG. Deutsche reported a 37 percent rise in operating earnings to 5.8 billion marks ($3.4 billion), Vereinsbank posted an 18 percent rise in operating profit to 1.6 billion marks.

"Deutsche's operating profit was strongly above our expectations -- around 800 million marks above it. We will certainly have to alter our earnings estimates for 1997 and 1998, and in part dramatically. It all depends on how lasting the effect can be. I cannot imagine that this comes from one particular element.
This more than confirms our positive view of the stock. (WestLB has Deutsche as strong buy) Obviously the operating side performed significantly better than expected.
There were no real surprises with Vereinsbank. It was generally within our expectations.

(On Deutsche) "The operating profit is clearly above expectations; there's a big divergence between net income and operating profit. It looks like Morgan Grenfell may be responsible. On balance the figures should confirm the market in its positive estimation of the stock. I am maintaining my buy (corrects from "hold") recommendation for three reasons: its strategy of cutting domestic costs, its clear presentation and implementation of cost reduction measures and also with a price earnings ratio of 15 based on 98 earnings it is fairly valued. I see its 1997 earnings per share rising to 5.10 marks followed by 5.60 marks in 1998. I am raising my estimate for 1996 EPS to 4.20 marks.
"I was surprised that (Vereinsbank's) risk provisions fell that much. I am maintaining my hold recommendation. The shares are too expensive from a fundamental point of view."
DIETER HEIN, BHF BANK AG, FRANKFURT

"Overall the banks have been able to increase their operating profits once again significantly -- which was something to be expected in general. The main factor was the fact that it was such a good year for financial markets. Generally own-account trading income rose considerably (except for Vereinsbank) and commission income had double digit increases.
At the same time administrative expenses were generally relatively low, except for banks like Deutsche and Dresdner which had to invest in U.K. investment banks.

The problem is that one can only speculate on the reason for the discrepancy between Deutsche Bank's operating profit and its net profit (2.1 billion marks). The tax rate must be a factor but cannot in itself be responsible. My interpretation is that this is connected to the Peter Young affair. Reserves could have been liquidated and placed on the operating account in order to finance the compensation.
(On Vereinsbank) Net interest income contributed and risk provisions were somewhat lower than expected."
